title: David-Horodok’s Jewish community destroyed by massacre and expulsion
summary: The mass murder of the town’s Jews, the killing of those still hiding, and the discovery of an empty town at liberation mark the destruction of the community.

Mass killing of women, men, and children
Michael Nosentschuk’s escape from the ghetto
Three hidden men were murdered en route to Stolin

editorialContent:
## The killings began with the men

The destruction of the [David-Horodok Jewish community](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_1ffa438353dc176e94f25c7d) unfolded in stages: men were seized and murdered, women and children were driven from their homes, and the survivors were eventually confined in a ghetto and killed or forced to flee. The [memorial book’s accounts](/communities/david-horodok/records/event_candidate_a79f8d2046f4576e040bfae9) preserve different dates and details; they do not yield one completely consistent chronology.

The first killings are remembered in one account as a July Aktion in which all the town’s men were murdered; another describes an early-August roundup. These may be different descriptions of the sequence, or differing recollections of its timing. The memorial book also records the killing of 53 people in 1941, including Jacob, Hannah’s father, and Gitl’s husband. That figure does not agree with the account describing thousands of victims, and the records do not explain whether the 53 refers to a separate incident.

The best-detailed account describes a mass killing of Jewish men aged fourteen and older. It says they were called to assemble under the pretext of forced labor, then marched to prepared graves near Hinavsk. Another account places the graves along the road between Chinovsk and Olshan. In the JewishGen translation, Michael Nosanchuk recalls hearing gunfire from Rubiel and dates the massacre to around the 16th of Av; the passage also gives August 10. A different memorial-book record gives August 16. The discrepancy should remain visible: the sources do not establish one uncontested Gregorian date or place.

Yad Vashem’s Encyclopedia of the Ghettos independently describes men aged fourteen and older being taken to pits near Olszany and murdered on August 10, 1941, by an SS cavalry unit. It records two children escaping and later reaching partisans. This broadly corroborates the memorial book’s account of the men’s murder, while differing from some of its date and location formulations. ([Yad Vashem, David-Horodok entry](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=224))

## A town emptied, families scattered

The memorial book names local collaborators as well as victims. Its account identifies Maraiko—also rendered Mareyke—as a local authority figure, and describes Germans and local men participating in the roundup and killing. One passage says [Jacob ben Abba Gratsulin](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_b41daceebb9e1a15bf33afc2) alone had been told the fate awaiting those being taken away; he was shot while trying to escape. [Leyb Trayster](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_ff01ba7bdb3eaa9610db99ee) is remembered as leading a group left to arrange bodies before they too were murdered. These are names preserved in a community’s testimony, not a complete roster of the dead.

After the men’s killing, women and children were ordered out of town. Some fled toward nearby places, including Stolin, Sarny, and Lachwa; others returned or had nowhere safe to go. Yad Vashem likewise records that hundreds reached nearby towns, while many could not find shelter and returned to David-Horodok. The same source says a ghetto was established in early 1942, with women and children forming most of its population. ([Yad Vashem](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=224))

The records also preserve individual attempts to survive. [Michael Nosentschuk’s escape](/communities/david-horodok/records/event_candidate_13a4ac26b31cc98227656ab9) was aided by a non-Jewish man who took him out of the ghetto. Another account tells of three hidden men—Kehat, Moses, and Abraham—murdered by non-Jews while traveling toward Stolin in 1943. Such stories show both the importance of flight and its terrible risks. The supplied records do not resolve the identities or later fates of every family member, nor do they provide a complete account of who escaped beyond the region.

## The ghetto’s last days

The memorial book describes a year of hunger, illness, and danger in the ghetto. One witness recalls a mother washing and dressing in clean clothes as she prepared for death on what she understood to be the final night. The passage is a stark record of fear, but it does not by itself establish the exact fate of her parents.

Yad Vashem provides a more precise account of the ghetto’s liquidation: on September 9, 1942, it says, 1,263 people remained, only 30 of them men. The ghetto was liquidated the following day; approximately 1,100 people were murdered at the killing site used for the men, while about 100 escaped, some joining Soviet partisan units. ([Yad Vashem](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=224)) The memorial book’s broader account likewise says that women and children were taken to the earlier killing place and shot, but does not give this same precise date and count.

The account leaves important questions open: the identities of the two children who escaped the first massacre, the woman partisan whose name and fate were not preserved, and the later paths of those who reached the forest. A town-wide story cannot restore every missing biography. The memorial book records survivors’ memories, but, as a work written by survivors, it cannot be treated as a complete register of all families or fates.

## Liberation without return

The Red Army liberated David-Horodok in 1944. The memorial book says that no living Jews were found in the town. The record of liberation is therefore not a story of a community returning home: it marks the end of occupation after the Jewish town had already been destroyed.

Some survivors visited afterward and found the town burned. A memorial-book account mentions Hershl Karman and his sons in connection with such a visit, though the wording does not clearly establish that every one of them was among the visitors. A separate account describes partisans burning Jewish houses so that local residents would not benefit from Jewish property. These memories point to a landscape stripped of homes as well as people, but do not establish the fate of every building or survivor.

The Independent sources found here add useful checks but remain limited. Yad Vashem’s ghetto encyclopedia corroborates the main sequence and supplies dates and figures that the memorial book’s witnesses do not consistently agree on. A general entry on Davyd-Haradok likewise summarizes the occupation and killings, but is not a separate witness account. ([Davyd-Haradok, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davyd-Haradok)) No town-specific article on this event was located in the YIVO Encyclopedia or the USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia in the searches conducted. The memorial book remains essential for the named people and remembered experiences; the gaps and disagreements are part of the record, not a license to fill them with certainty.
